title: Castano v. American Tobacco Co.
lead: A nationwide tobacco class proposed resolving common conduct and punitive damages first, before the legal and individual issues of a new addiction-injury theory were understood.

actors.name: Castano and other smoker or survivor representatives
actors.role: Plaintiffs proposing a nationwide addiction class

proceedings: District court denied equitable-class certification but conditionally certified core liability and punitive issues under Rule 23(b)(3).
Fifth Circuit took a § 1292(b) appeal and reversed with instructions to dismiss the class complaint.
limits: The opinion did not determine individual tobacco liability or later settlements. Medical-monitoring certification denial was not appealed. Several due-process, Erie, Article III, and alternative predominance theories were expressly reserved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The plaintiffs plead addiction itself as a compensable injury
sections.cue: The class combines decades and different kinds of claims
paragraphs: Plaintiffs alleged that tobacco companies and the Tobacco Institute concealed nicotine’s addictive nature and manipulated levels to sustain dependence. Their nationwide proposed class included dependent cigarette purchasers and smokers, estates and representatives, and relatives or significant others claiming as heirs or survivors, reaching back to 1943. Current smokers served as representatives; Dianne Castano sued for her deceased husband.

Nine causes of action included fraud, negligent misrepresentation, emotional-distress and negligence theories, consumer protection, warranties, strict liability, and Louisiana redhibition. Requested relief included compensation, punitive damages, fees, notice, restitution or disgorgement, and medical monitoring. Plaintiffs conceded that addiction had to be proved individually. Concealment, manipulation, and causation remained allegations.

sections.title: A proposed multistage trial receives partial approval
paragraphs: Plaintiffs proposed a first jury trial of common conduct and core liability, sample cases to estimate compensation and a punitive ratio, individual claim verification and defenses, and final application of the ratio and reasonableness review. Treatment of personal injuries and individual proof remained uncertain.

The district court found Rule 23(a) satisfied but denied Rule 23(b)(2) equitable certification, including medical monitoring; plaintiffs did not cross-appeal. Under Rule 23(b)(3), it separated core liability, injury/causation/reliance/defenses, compensation, and punitive damages. It conditionally certified only core liability and punitive issues under Rule 23(c)(4), incorporating parts but not all of plaintiffs’ proposal.

The judge thought one conduct trial would advance all cases, relying on asbestos precedents, deferred detailed state-law and reliance issues, and read Eisen as preventing inquiry beyond pleadings into merits. Its punitive analysis also relied on a vacated Watson panel opinion lacking precedential force. Defendants obtained § 1292(b) interlocutory review, before later Rule 23(f).

sections.title: The Fifth Circuit requires law and trial analysis before certification
sections.cue: Conditional status does not postpone the initial burden
paragraphs: Judge Jerry E. Smith, joined by Duhé and DeMoss, identified independent failures to examine state-law variation and how the claims would actually be tried. Plaintiffs bore the burden of rigorous Rule 23 analysis despite broad trial-court discretion. Conditional certification permitted adjustments to unforeseen developments, not approval first and predominance later.

Limited state surveys, a jury form, and other certification citations did not show manageable treatment of reliance, disclosure, strict liability, assumption of risk, comparative fault, emotional distress, and other differences. Multistate classes were not categorically forbidden; sufficient grouping and analysis could work. The court even acknowledged that common issues might ultimately predominate despite smoking-history differences. The missing inquiry, not a complete appellate choice-of-law determination, was the error.

Jenkins’s 893 asbestos cases under one state’s law in one district did not establish manageability for this nationwide, multitheory, multidefendant, fifty-year dispute. Comparison to millions of hypothetical suits skipped analysis of the actual proposed process.

sections.title: A common question is not necessarily a predominant one
sections.cue: The immature theory independently defeats superiority at this stage
paragraphs: Eisen and Miller prohibited deciding certification based on perceived likelihood of merits victory, not examining facts and law needed to apply Rule 23. The significance of defendants’ conduct depended on individual reliance, causation, addiction, and defenses. Postponing reliance analysis might reveal after a class trial that certification was never proper. Under this court’s historical reading of Rule 23(c)(4), isolating a common issue could not manufacture predominance before the cause as a whole met Rule 23(b)(3).

The untested addiction-as-injury theory lacked useful individual-trial experience. Nationwide aggregation risked extraordinary, industry-threatening settlement pressure without established proof patterns. That was not a categorical ban on mass tort classes. A litigation crisis was speculative, and individual suits might be viable through substantial damages, punitive relief, or fees. Earlier tobacco failures alone did not justify aggregation. Individual cases and coordinated discovery could clarify theories and state law.

Efficiency was uncertain because conduct evidence might recur in reliance or comparative-fault trials, and premature certification could consume years before decertification. Later juries comparing fault might reexamine the first jury’s findings, creating a substantial Seventh Amendment separability problem, not a ban on all bifurcation. Urgency did not cure it: medical monitoring had been denied without appeal, survivors were included, and class proceedings followed by individual ones could delay recovery.

sections.title: The class complaint must be dismissed
sections.cue: Individual liability and reserved constitutional objections remain open
paragraphs: On May 23, 1996, the Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded with instructions to dismiss the class complaint. Because immaturity independently defeated superiority then, another immediate certification attempt could not cure the identified errors. The court awarded no damages and did not adjudicate each smoker’s individual claim.

It expressly left other attacks undecided, including due process concerning the punitive ratio, categorical Erie and Article III objections, and defendants’ alternative predominance theory. Subsequent tobacco settlements were not the disposition of this 1996 appeal.
